newsitem.title: ITALY: Egypt backs U.S. as 'honest broker' in Mideast.
newsitem.headline: Egypt backs U.S. as 'honest broker' in Mideast.

text.p: Egypt said on Wednesday the United States had to continue to play the role of "honest broker" to try to save the Middle East peace process and welcomed a strong statement by the European Union urging a resumption of talks.
"The United States role is important as the sponsor of the process that started in Madrid (in 1991) and that process is not dead, is not yet dead," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said in Rome.
"Therefore it (the process) has to continue with the principal...sponsors, trying to save it, to push it forward," he told a joint news conference with Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini.

Moussa was in Rome at the start of a visit to Italy, France and Britain to try to muster European support for Egypt's attempts to break a three-month-old stall in talks between Israel and the Palestinians.

He spoke of a "serious deterioration" in the peace process, but neither he nor Dini announced any specific initiative to end the impasse, which has persisted since Israel decided to press ahead with a Jewish settlement project in Arab East Jerusalem.
Arab states have looked to the Europeans to balance a perceived U.S. bias towards Israel and to press Washington to take a more active role in breaking the deadlock.

Palestinian suspicions were reinforced last week by a 406-17 vote in the U.S. House of Representatives on a non-binding resolution calling on President Bill Clinton to reaffirm that Jerusalem must remain Israel's "undivided capital".
Meanwhile scores of mostly teenage Palestinians have been shot and wounded by Israeli troops in the West Bank town of Hebron during the past four days of violent protests in the divided town.
Egypt was the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with the Jewish state and it receives some $2bn in civil and military aid each year from Washington.
Moussa described the U.S. resolution as "unwise (and) uncalled for" but noted that official U.S. policy was that the final status of Jerusalem had to be settled by the two parties.
"As for the U.S. role, it should continue on the basis of, or from the standpoint of, an honest broker," he said.
He also welcomed a statement adopted by EU leaders at their Amsterdam summit which urged Israel for the first time to consider allowing the creation of a Palestinian state.

The "European Call for Peace in the Middle East" warned that stagnation on the Palestinian, Syrian and Lebanese negotiating tracks "is a permanent threat to the security of all" and urged the peoples and governments of the Middle East to renew talks.

"The declaration of the European Union of such a position taken...in order to save the process will have a beneficial effect, a very useful effect on the substance of the process of peace," Moussa said.
Dini said the statement was an indication of the strength of European interest in Middle East peace, adding that the first priority was a resumption of Israeli-Palestinian talks.
"We are all deeply concerned at the fact that the peace process with Israel...has come in a way to a complete stop with grave dangers to the region itself and the peoples of the region," Dini said.
He said in response to a question that he did not regard the EU statement as a potential hindrance.

Israeli leaders have long told the EU that by calling publicly for a Palestinian state, they were prejudging the outcome of negotiations and taking sides in the Arab-Israeli dispute in a way that disqualified Europe as an honest broker.
